claim: Rats expressing AAV1-CaMKIIa-ArchT-GFP or AAV8-CAMKIIa-GFP in the perirhinal cortex underwent object cue conditioning to learn the outcomes associated with appetitive, aversive, and neutral object pairs.
source: Rats expressing AAV1-CaMKIIa-ArchT-GFP (archaerhodopsin T [ArchT]) or AAV8-CAMKIIa-GFP (green fluorescent protein [GFP]) in the perirhinal cortex (PRC, a) underwent object cue conditioning to learn the outcomes associated with appetitive (APP), aversive (AV), and neutral (NEU) object pairs (b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the figure caption and supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: Three-way ANOVA of acquisition data indicated successful learning in both ArchT and GFP groups.
source: Three-way ANOVA of acquisition data (mean ± SEM) indicated successful learning in both ArchT and GFP groups (c).
evidence: Statistical analysis results are explicitly stated in the figure caption and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PRC groups acquired the object-outcome associations successfully by test 2, with rats spending the most time in the goal box after exposure to the appetitive object pair (p<0.001), and the least time after aversive object pair exposure (p<0.001), compared to goal box time in neutral trials.
source: PRC groups acquired the object-outcome associations successfully by test 2, with rats spending the most time in the goal box after exposure to the appetitive object pair (p<0.001), and the least time after aversive object pair exposure (p<0.001), compared to goal box time in neutral trials (valence: F(2,40)=396.99, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.95).
evidence: Statistical test results with p-values and effect sizes are provided, demonstrating successful acquisition of object-outcome associations.

claim: Rats exhibited a significant reduction in goal box time during aversive test session between the two acquisition tests.
source: Rats also exhibited a significant reduction in goal box time during aversive test session between the two acquisition tests (valence × test: F(2,40)=16.86, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.46) (Figure 1c).
evidence: Statistical interaction effect is reported with specific F-statistic, p-value, and effect size.

claim: The pattern of valence acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals.
source: The pattern of valence acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,20)=1.51, p=0.23, ηp2 = 0.07; valence × construct: F(2,40)=1.1, p=0.34, ηp2 = 0.05; test × construct: F(2,40)=0.2, p=0.66, ηp2 = 0.01).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no difference between groups during acquisition.

claim: When animals were exposed to a high conflict object pair, optogenetic inhibition of PRC significantly increased time spent in the goal box compared with trials completed without inhibition, and compared to GFP control animals with laser on and off.
source: When animals were exposed to a high conflict object pair, optogenetic inhibition of PRC (laser on) significantly increased time spent in the goal box compared with trials completed without inhibition (laser off), and compared to GFP control animals with laser on and off (laser × construct: F(1,20)=40.73, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.67; all post hoc: p<0.001) (Figure 2b)
evidence: Statistical analysis with significant interaction effect and post-hoc comparisons demonstrate the effect of PRC inhibition on approach behavior.

claim: An analysis of the 'difference score' between the two conflict test sessions indicated that laser-treated ArchT animals spent more time in the goal box than GFP animals.
source: An analysis of the 'difference score' between the two conflict test sessions (i.e., laser on–laser off) also indicated that laser-treated ArchT animals spent more time in the goal box than GFP animals (ArchT: 29.72 (M)±14.23 (SD), GFP: –1.41±8.37, t(20) = 6.38, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of difference scores with t-test results demonstrates significant effect of PRC inhibition.

claim: PRC inhibition led to a significant decrease in the number of retreats from the goal box.
source: Furthermore, PRC inhibition led to a significant decrease in the number of retreats from the goal box (laser × construct: F(1,20)=24.08, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.55)
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant interaction effect on retreat behavior.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the number of goal box entries during the choice period.
source: although there was no effect on the number of goal box entries (laser × construct: F(1,20) = 3.12, p=0.09, ηp2 = 0.14) (Figure 2c) during the choice period.
evidence: Non-significant statistical result indicates no effect on entry behavior.

claim: PRC inhibition had no impact on the latency to enter each of the object, neutral and goal boxes.
source: PRC inhibition also had no impact on the latency to enter (LTE) each of the object, neutral and goal boxes (laser × construct: F(1,20) = 2.24, p=0.15, ηp2 = 0.1; laser × construct × box: F(2,40)=0.47, p=0.63, ηp2 = 0.02)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on latency measures.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the exploration of appetitive and aversive objects.
source: nor did it have an effect on the exploration of appetitive and aversive objects (laser × construct: F(1,20) = 3.10, p=0.09, ηp2 = 0.13; laser × construct × object: F(1,20)=0.15, p=0.70, ηp2 = 0.007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on object exploration.

claim: When faced with high motivational conflict, PRC-inhibited rats entered the goal box as readily as control animals but stayed longer and retreated less, indicative of a potentiated approach bias under conflict.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that when faced with high motivational conflict, PRC-inhibited rats entered the goal box as readily as control animals but stayed longer and retreated less, indicative of a potentiated approach bias under conflict.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the data results presented earlier in the text.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the time spent in the goal box after exploring neutral objects.
source: This effect was not observed in the neutral object test: PRC inhibition had no effect on the time spent in the goal box after exploring neutral objects (laser × construct: F(1,18)=1.02, p=0.33, ηp2 = 0.05) (Figure 2d).
evidence: Non-significant statistical result indicates no effect in neutral condition.

claim: When PRC-inhibited animals were exposed to 'low conflict' object pairs (appetitive-neutral and aversive-neutral), their time in the goal box increased.
source: When PRC-inhibited animals were exposed to 'low conflict' object pairs (appetitive-neutral and aversive-neutral), their time in the goal box increased (laser × construct: F(1,16)=9.37, p=0.007, ηp2 = 0.37) (Figure 2e)
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant interaction effect on goal box time in low conflict condition.

claim: There was no corresponding increase in the number of entries into or retreats from the goal box during the choice period in low conflict tests.
source: but there was no corresponding increase in the number of entries into (laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.47, p=0.50, ηp2 = 0.02) or retreats from (laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.54, p=0.47, ηp2 = 0.04) the goal box during the choice period (Figure 2f–g).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on entries or retreats in low conflict condition.

claim: Laser treatment increased goal box time for ArchT animals compared with GFP when faced with both App-Neu and Av-Neu pairings.
source: An analysis of the difference score (laser on–laser off) for the two low conflict tests revealed that laser treatment increased goal box time for ArchT animals compared with GFP, when faced with both App-Neu (ArchT: 22.13 (M)±21.61 (SD), GFP: 1.81±7.49, Mann-Whitney U=15, p=0.027, two-tailed) and Av-Neu (ArchT: 13.32±8.45, GFP: 1.07±10.77, t(16) = 2.71, p=0.016) pairings.
evidence: Statistical comparisons of difference scores show significant effects for both low conflict conditions.

claim: PRC inhibition did not impair the ability to discriminate appetitive and aversive valences.
source: Notably, PRC inhibition did not impair the ability to discriminate appetitive and aversive valences (valence: F(1,16)=229.64, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.94; laser × valence × construct: F(1,16)=1.14, p=0.3, ηp2 = 0.07), with all animals spending significantly more time in the goal box for appetitive-neutral pairings than aversive-neutral (p<0.001, Figure 2e).
evidence: Statistical results show intact valence discrimination despite PRC inhibition.

claim: All PRC rats made fewer entries and exhibited more retreat behavior when presented with an aversive-neutral pairing compared with an appetitive-neutral pairing.
source: Furthermore, all PRC rats made fewer entries (p=0.039) and exhibited more retreat behavior (p<0.0001) when presented with an aversive-neutral pairing compared with an appetitive-neutral pairing (Figure 2f–g), indicating that valence recall was intact in PRC-inhibited rats.
evidence: Statistical comparisons demonstrate differential behavior based on valence, indicating intact valence recall.

claim: Animals acquired the cue-outcome associations successfully by the first test, and spent significantly more time in the goal box after exposure to the appetitive object pairs compared with the aversive pairs.
source: Animals acquired the cue-outcome associations successfully by the first test, and spent significantly more time in the goal box after exposure to the appetitive object pairs compared with the aversive pairs, with comparable acquisition behavior between sets of objects pairs within each valence (valence: F(1,14)=259.27, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.95; pairing: F(1,14)=1.67, p=0.22, ηp2 = 0.11; valence × pairing: F(1,14)=0.27, p=0.61, ηp2 = 0.02; Figure 3b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition of object-outcome associations in the no conflict recombination task.

claim: The pattern of object cue acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the no conflict recombination task.
source: The pattern of object cue acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,14)=0.16, p=0.69, ηp2 = 0.01; pairing × construct: F(1,14)=0.04, p=0.86, ηp2 = 0.003).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no group differences in acquisition.

claim: PRC inhibition did not lead to significant changes in the time spent in the goal box after exposure to novel appetitive or aversive object pairs in the no conflict recombination test.
source: Rats were then administered a within-valence 'no conflict' recombination test (appetitive-appetitive; aversive-aversive). PRC inhibition did not lead to significant changes in the time spent in the goal box after exposure to novel appetitive or aversive object pairs (laser: F(1,14)=0.10, p=0.76, ηp2 = 0.007; laser × construct: F(1,14)=0.01, p=0.92, ηp2 = 0.001) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect of PRC inhibition in no conflict condition.

claim: Laser treatment had no effect on goal box time when animals encountered either App-App or Av-Av pairings in the no conflict test.
source: An analysis of the difference score (laser on–laser off) for the two respective no conflict tests revealed that laser treatment had no effect on goal box time when animals encountered either App-App (ArchT: 0.65 (M)±9.27 (SD), GFP: –1.81±16.33, t(14)=0.37, p=0.72) or Av-Av (ArchT: –1.97 (M)±19.80 (SD), GFP: –0.72±12.54, t(14) = –0.15, p<0.88) pairings.
evidence: Statistical comparisons of difference scores show no significant effects in no conflict condition.

claim: Both ArchT and GFP animals readily discriminated between valences during the no conflict test.
source: Furthermore, both ArchT and GFP animals readily discriminated between valences during this test (valence: F(1,14) = 371.95, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.96; valence × construct: F(1,14)=0.05, p=0.82, ηp2 = 0.004).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in no conflict condition.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the number of entries into nor retreats from the goal box in the no conflict test.
source: PRC inhibition also had no effect on the number of entries into (laser × construct: F(1,14)=0.06, p=0.82, ηp2 = 0.004) nor retreats from the goal box (laser × construct: F(1,14)=0.15, p=0.71, ηp2 = 0.01)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on entries or retreats in no conflict condition.

claim: All PRC-inhibited rats made fewer entries and exhibited more retreat behavior when presented with an aversive pairing compared with an appetitive pairing in the no conflict test.
source: and furthermore, all PRC-inhibited rats made fewer entries (p<0.001) and exhibited more retreat behavior (p<0.0001) when presented with an aversive pairing compared with an appetitive pairing (Figure 3d–e).
evidence: Statistical comparisons show differential behavior based on valence in no conflict condition.

claim: When faced with high conflict, PRC inhibition led to animals spending significantly more time by the sucrose dispenser compared to high conflict test sessions without optogenetic inhibition.
source: When faced with high conflict, PRC inhibition led to animals spending significantly more time by the sucrose dispenser compared to high conflict test sessions without optogenetic inhibition (p<0.0001), whereas an increase in time spent by the dispenser elicited by low conflict stimuli approached significance (p=0.052; laser: F(1,18)=24.34, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.57; laser × conflict: F(2,32)=5.43, p=0.0093, ηp2 = 0.25) (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition on time spent near reward location.

claim: In the absence of PRC inhibition, animals spent more time by the dispenser during no conflict trials compared to high conflict and low conflict trials.
source: As expected, in the absence of PRC inhibition, animals spent more time by the dispenser during no conflict trials compared to high conflict (p=0.002) and low conflict (p=0.03) trials.
evidence: Statistical comparisons show differential behavior across conflict levels without PRC inhibition.

claim: PRC-inhibited rats spent a higher proportion of time at the dispenser during high conflict trials compared with low conflict and no conflict trials, as well as high conflict trials completed with the laser off.
source: When considering the time spent by the dispenser as a proportion of the total time in the goal box, PRC-inhibited rats spent a higher proportion of time at the dispenser during high conflict trials compared with low conflict (p=0.0008) and no conflict (p=0.0012) trials, as well as high conflict trials completed with the laser off (p=0.015; laser: F(1,18)=7.80, p=0.012, ηp2 = 0.30, conflict: F(1.79,28.65)=11.19, p=0.00038, ηp2 = 0.41, laser × conflict: F(2,32)=3.34, p=0.048, ηp2 = 0.17) (Figure 4c).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effects on proportional time spent near reward location.

claim: Laser off animals spent proportionally more time by the dispenser during no conflict trials compared with low conflict trials, with no difference between no conflict and high conflict trials.
source: Laser off animals also spent proportionally more time by the dispenser during no conflict trials compared with low conflict trials (p=0.017), with no difference between no conflict and high conflict trials (p=0.89).
evidence: Statistical comparisons show differential behavior across conflict levels without PRC inhibition.

claim: Animals were significantly faster to enter all compartments under 'laser on' conditions, which was likely driven by the PRC inhibition group data.
source: To further investigate the impact of PRC inhibition on reward approach, we also analyzed the LTE into the object, neutral and goal boxes across the two levels of conflict that included an appetitive object (e.g., App+Av; App+Neu). Animals were significantly faster to enter all compartments under 'laser on' conditions (laser: F(1,16)=9.67, p=0.007, ηp2 = 0.38), which was likely driven by the PRC inhibition group data (laser × construct: F(1,16)=3.92, p=0.065, ηp2 = 0.20; laser × construct × box × conflict: F(2,32)=0.2, p=0.82; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 a,c).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows effect of laser treatment on latency to enter compartments.

claim: All rats exhibited longer latencies to enter the boxes during the high conflict condition, compared with the low conflict test.
source: However, all rats exhibited longer latencies to enter the boxes during the high conflict condition, compared with the low conflict test (conflict: F(1,16)=10.47, p<0.005, ηp2 = 0.40).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows main effect of conflict level on latency.

claim: Object exploration was comparable between high vs. low conflict conditions, with PRC inhibition having no impact on the durations of object exploration.
source: Object exploration was also comparable between high vs. low conflict conditions, with PRC inhibition having no impact on the durations of object exploration (conflict: F(1,16)=0.003, p=0.96, ηp2 = 0.0001; laser: F(1,16)=0.034, p=0.86, ηp2 = 0.002; laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.056, p=0.82, ηp2 = 0.003).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on object exploration.

claim: The observed involvement of the PRC in the arbitration of AA conflict arises from alterations in conflict processing, rather than impairments in valence retrieval or novel stimulus recombination processing.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that the PRC inhibition-induced increase in approach behavior during the high and low conflict tests arises from alterations in conflict processing, rather than impairments in valence retrieval or novel stimulus recombination processing.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the data results presented earlier in the text.

claim: In the absence of the normal PRC functioning, animals spent more time by the sucrose dispenser and traversed through the runway more quickly, reflecting a greater anticipation for a reward outcome.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of the normal PRC functioning, animals spent more time by the sucrose dispenser and traversed through the runway more quickly, reflecting a greater anticipation for a reward outcome.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the behavioral data.

claim: All animals demonstrated object-outcome associations by acquisition test 2 in the separate cohort with post-object exploration inhibition.
source: All rats acquired the object-outcome associations successfully by test 2, with rats spending the most time in the goal box after exposure to the appetitive object pair (p<0.001), and the least time after aversive object pair exposure (p<0.001), compared to goal box time in neutral trials (valence: F(2,28)=231.3, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.94; Figure 5b)
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition in the control cohort.

claim: Rats exhibited a significant increase in goal box time during appetitive trials and decrease in aversive trials between the two acquisition tests in the control cohort.
source: rats exhibited a significant increase in goal box time during appetitive trials and decrease in aversive trials between the two acquisition tests (valence × test: F(2,28)=54.91, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.80).
evidence: Statistical interaction effect demonstrates learning across acquisition tests.

claim: The pattern of valence acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the control cohort.
source: The pattern of valence acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,14)=1.09, p=0.3, ηp2 = 0.07; valence × construct: F(2, 28)=1.53, p=0.23, ηp2 = 0.10; test × construct: F(1, 14)=1.64, p=0.22, ηp2 = 0.10).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no group differences in acquisition.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PRC prior to goal box access significantly increased time spent in the goal box compared to trials without inhibition, and compared to GFP control animals.
source: When animals were exposed to a high conflict object pair, optogenetic inhibition of PRC prior to goal box access significantly increased time spent in the goal box compared to trials without inhibition, and compared to GFP control animals (laser × construct: F(1,14)=81.3, p<0.001, ηp2=0.85; all post hoc: p<0.001) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition during choice period.

claim: Turning the laser on following neutral box entry did not impact time spent in the goal box when compared with animals that received whole-session laser application.
source: Turning the laser on following neutral box entry did not impact time spent in the goal box when compared with animals that received whole-session laser application (laser timing: F(1,34)=1.26, p=0.27, ηp2=0.04; laser timing × laser: F(1,34)=0.06, p=0.81, ηp2=0.002; laser timing × construct: F(1, 34)=0.12, p=0.7, ηp2=0.005)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no difference between timing conditions.

claim: PRC mediates object-based motivational conflict rather than encoding or retrieving representations of highly conflicting objects.
source: suggesting that PRC mediates object-based motivational conflict rather than encoding or retrieving representations of highly conflicting objects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of whole-session vs. choice-period inhibition results.

claim: The difference score of the two conflict test sessions revealed that laser treatment increased goal box time for ArchT animals only in the control cohort.
source: The difference score of the two conflict test sessions (laser on–laser off) revealed that laser treatment increased goal box time for ArchT animals only (ArchT: 32.13±5.95, GFP: –2.22±8.98, t(14) = 9.02, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of difference scores demonstrates specific effect in ArchT group.

claim: PRC inhibition during the choice period led to a significant decrease in the number of retreats from the goal box.
source: PRC inhibition during the choice period led to a significant decrease in the number of retreats from the goal box (laser × construct: F(1,14) = 38.11, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.73)
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect on retreat behavior.

claim: PRC inhibition during the choice period had no effect on the number of goal box entries.
source: while having no effect on the number of goal box entries (laser × construct: F(1,14)=0.88, p=0.37, ηp2 = 0.06) (Figure 5d)
evidence: Non-significant statistical result indicates no effect on entry behavior.

claim: PRC inhibition during the choice period had no effect on the time spent in the goal box during the neutral object test.
source: PRC inhibition had no effect on the time spent in the goal box during the neutral object test (laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.87, p=0.37, ηp2 = 0.07; Figure 5e).
evidence: Non-significant statistical result indicates no effect in neutral condition.

claim: Inhibiting PRC during the choice period increased the time spent in the goal box for both App-Neu and Av-Neu object pairs in the low conflict test.
source: Similar to rats that received whole-session PRC inhibition, inhibiting PRC during the choice period increased the time spent in the goal box for both App-Neu and Av-Neu object pairs (laser × construct: F(1,14)=15.77, p<0.005, ηp2=0.53) (Figure 5f).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect in low conflict condition.

claim: The laser treatment difference score analysis showed that ArchT animals spent more time in the goal box when faced with App-Neu, but not Av-Neu pairings.
source: The laser treatment difference score analysis showed that ArchT animals spent more time in the goal box when faced with App-Neu (ArchT: 22.58±11.72, GFP: –0.34±9.22, t(14) = 4.35, p=0.001), but not Av-Neu (ArchT: 13.17±15.35, GFP: 0.40±16.71, t(14) = 1.59, p=0.13) pairings.
evidence: Statistical comparisons of difference scores show differential effects for different low conflict conditions.

claim: PRC inhibition during the choice period did not impair the ability to discriminate appetitive and aversive valences in the low conflict test.
source: Notably, PRC inhibition during the choice period did not impair the ability to discriminate appetitive and aversive valences (valence: F(1,14)=253.86, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.95; laser × valence × construct: F(1,14)=1.0, p=0.34, ηp2 = 0.07), with all animals spending significantly more time in the goal box for appetitive-neutral pairings than aversive-neutral (p<0.001, Figure 5f).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination.

claim: All PRC rats made fewer entries and exhibited more retreat behavior when presented with an aversive-neutral pairing compared with an appetitive-neutral pairing in the control cohort low conflict test.
source: Furthermore, all PRC rats made fewer entries (p=0.001) and exhibited more retreat behavior (p<0.001) when presented with an aversive-neutral pairing compared with an appetitive-neutral pairing (Figure 5g–h). Thus, valence recall was intact in PRC-inhibited rats.
evidence: Statistical comparisons demonstrate differential behavior based on valence.

claim: PRC-inhibited ArchT animals spent significantly more time by the sucrose dispenser after encountering both high conflict and low conflict stimuli, compared to test sessions without optogenetic inhibition.
source: Finally, PRC-inhibited ArchT animals spent significantly more time by the sucrose dispenser after encountering both high conflict (p<0.001) and low conflict (p<0.01) stimuli, compared to test sessions without optogenetic inhibition (laser: F(1,7)=130.11, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.95; laser × conflict: F(1,7)=10.70, p=0.014, ηp2 = 0.61) (Figure 5i).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effects on time spent near reward location in control cohort.

claim: PRC-inhibited rats spent a higher proportion of time by the dispenser during high conflict trials compared with low conflict trials, as well as high conflict trials completed with the laser off in the control cohort.
source: PRC-inhibited rats also spent a higher proportion of time by the dispenser during high conflict trials compared with low conflict (p<0.0001) trials, as well as high conflict trials completed with the laser off (p=0.001; laser: F(1, 7)=34.10, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.83; conflict: F(1,7)=24.41, p=0.002, ηp2 = 0.78; laser × conflict: F(1,7)=5.95, p=0.045, ηp2 = 0.46) (Figure 5j).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effects on proportional time spent near reward location in control cohort.

claim: PRC inhibition during the choice period did not change LTE behavior in the control cohort.
source: An analysis of the LTE data for each of the boxes between high and low conflict sessions revealed that PRC inhibition did not change LTE behavior (laser: F(1,14)=0.803, p=0.39, ηp2 = 0.05; laser × construct: F(1,14)=1.48, p=0.24, ηp2 = 0.1)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on latency to enter.

claim: All rats exhibited overall longer latencies to enter all boxes during the high conflict test compared with the low conflict test in the control cohort.
source: with all rats exhibiting overall longer latencies to enter all boxes during the high conflict test compared with the low conflict test (p=0.043; conflict: F(1,14)=9.99, p=0.007, ηp2 = 0.42; construct: F(1,14)=0.17, p=0.69, ηp2 = 0.01; conflict × construct: F(1,14)=0.28, p=0.60, ηp2 = 0.02; laser × construct × box × conflict: F(2,28)=0.16, p=0.85).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows main effect of conflict level on latency.

claim: PRC rats demonstrated the expected behavior by test 2 in the shuttle box task, with rats exhibiting significantly shorter escape latencies after exposure to the aversive object pair compared with exposure to the appetitive object pair.
source: PRC rats demonstrated the expected behavior by test 2, with rats exhibiting significantly shorter escape latencies after exposure to the aversive object pair compared with exposure to the appetitive object pair (valence: F(1,13)=45.97, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.78; valence × test: F(1,13)=16.17, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.55) (Figure 6d).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition of escape behavior in shuttle box task.

claim: The pattern of escape acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the shuttle box task.
source: The pattern of escape acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,13)=4.55, p=0.052, ηp2 = 0.26; valence × construct: F(1,13)=4.22, p=0.06, ηp2 = 0.25; test × construct: F(1,13)=2.69, p=0.13, ηp2 = 0.17).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no group differences in escape acquisition.

claim: PRC rats spent more time in the outcome-associated area when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair in the shuttle box task.
source: PRC rats also spent more time in the outcome-associated area (stay behavior) when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair (valence: F(1,13)=456.04, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; valence × test: F(1,13)=21.18, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.62) (Figure 6e).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates differential stay behavior based on valence.

claim: The pattern of stay behavior was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the shuttle box task.
source: This pattern of stay behavior was also comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,13)=3.57, p=0.082, ηp2 = 0.22; valence × construct: F(1,13)=8.17, p=0.013, ηp2 = 0.39; test × construct: F(1,13)=1.65, p=0.22, ηp2 = 0.11).
evidence: Statistical results indicate generally comparable stay behavior between groups.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PRC significantly prolonged escape latencies compared with trials completed without inhibition, and compared to GFP control animals with laser on and off in the shuttle box high conflict test.
source: When animals were next exposed to a high conflict pairing, optogenetic inhibition of PRC (laser on) significantly prolonged escape latencies compared with trials completed without inhibition (laser off; p<0.001), and compared to GFP control animals (p<0.005) with laser on and off (laser × construct: F(1,13)=18.97, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.59) (Figure 6f)
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition on escape latency in shuttle box.

claim: PRC-inhibited animals spent significantly longer in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair compared with trials completed without inhibition, and compared to GFP control animals with laser on and off.
source: Furthermore, despite making a comparable number of re-entries into the outcome-associated area during the test session (laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.99, p=0.34, ηp2 = 0.07), PRC-inhibited animals spent significantly longer in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair compared with trials completed without inhibition (laser off; p<0.001), and compared to GFP control animals (p<0.005) with laser on and off (laser × construct: F(1,13)=12.32, p=0.004, ηp2 = 0.49) (Figure 6g).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition on time spent in outcome-associated area.

claim: Laser treatment both decreased escape latency and increased cumulative duration in the outcome-associated area for ArchT animals compared with GFP in the shuttle box high conflict test.
source: An analysis of the difference score of the two conflict test sessions (laser on–laser off) revealed that laser treatment both decreased escape latency (ArchT: 32.91±19.85, GFP: –1.54±9.8, Mann-Whitney U=2, ArchT = 7, GFP = 8, p=0.001, two-tailed), and increased cumulative duration in the outcome-associated area (ArchT: 50.04±36.64, GFP: –1.57±18.70, Mann-Whitney U=7, p=0.014, two-tailed) for ArchT animals compared with GFP.
evidence: Statistical comparisons of difference scores demonstrate specific effects in ArchT group.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the duration of escape latencies for either appetitive or aversive valences in the shuttle box control test.
source: PRC inhibition had no effect on the duration of escape latencies, defined as the length of the first 'stay' only in the cued side, for either appetitive or aversive valences (laser: F(1,13)=0.88, p=0.37, ηp2 = 0.06; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.15, p=0.71, ηp2 = 0.01; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.04, p=0.84, ηp2 = 0.003), with all rats exhibiting significantly shorter escape latencies for aversive than appetitive trials (valence: F(1,13)=84.84, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.87; construct: F(1,13)=0.06, p=0.82, ηp2 = 0.004) (Figure 6h).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in shuttle box control test.

claim: PRC inhibition had no effect on the amount of time spent in the cued side of the apparatus in the shuttle box control test.
source: Similarly, PRC inhibition had no effect on the amount of time spent in the cued side of the apparatus, defined as the total time spent across multiple stays in the chamber (laser: F(1,13)=0.59, p=0.46, ηp2 = 0.04; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.003, p=0.96, ηp2 < 0.001; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.22, p=0.65, ηp2 = 0.02), with all rats spending significantly less time in the cued side during aversive than appetitive trials (valence: F(1,13)=470.47, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; construct: F(1,13)=0.55, p=0.47, ηp2 = 0.04) (Figure 6i).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in shuttle box control test.

claim: PRC inhibition led to both a decrease in avoidance behavior and/or an increase in approach/stay behavior under motivational conflict in the shuttle box task.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that PRC inhibition led to both a decrease in avoidance behavior and/or an increase in approach/stay behavior under motivational conflict, and that PRC-inhibited animals could readily discriminate between appetitive and aversive object cues.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the shuttle box results.

claim: All rats exhibited significantly shorter escape latencies after exposure to the aversive object pair compared with exposure to the appetitive object pair by the second acquisition test in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: All rats exhibited significantly shorter escape latencies after exposure to the aversive object pair compared with exposure to the appetitive object pair by the second acquisition test (valence: F(1,14)=123.22, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.9; valence × test: F(1,14)=116.05, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.89) (Figure 7b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition in shuttle box control cohort.

claim: The pattern of escape acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: The pattern of escape acquisition was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,14)=0.23, p=0.63, ηp2 = 0.02; valence × construct: F(1,14)=0.04, p=0.85, ηp2 = 0.003; test × construct: F(1,14)=1.06, p=0.32, ηp2 = 0.07).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no group differences in acquisition.

claim: Rats spent more time in the outcome-associated area when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: Rats also spent more time in the outcome-associated area (stay behavior) when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair (valence: F(1,14)=419.32, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; valence × test: F(1,14)=140.61, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.91) (Figure 7b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates differential stay behavior based on valence.

claim: The pattern of stay behavior was comparable between ArchT and GFP animals in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: This pattern of stay behavior was also comparable between ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,9)=2.66, p=0.13, ηp2 = 0.23; valence × construct: F(1,14)=0.35, p=0.56, ηp2 = 0.02; test × construct: F(1,14)=0.95, p=0.35, ηp2 = 0.06).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no group differences in stay behavior.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of PRC during the choice period significantly prolonged escape latencies in the shuttle box control cohort high conflict test.
source: When animals were exposed to a high conflict object pair, optogenetic inhibition of PRC (laser on) during the choice period significantly prolonged escape latencies compared with trials completed without inhibition (laser off; p<0.001), and compared to GFP control animals (p<0.001) with laser on and off (laser × construct: F(1,14)=47.74, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.77) (Figure 7c)
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition during choice period in shuttle box.

claim: PRC-inhibited animals spent significantly longer in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair during the choice period in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: Furthermore, despite making a comparable number of re-entries into the outcome-associated area during the test session (laser × construct: F(1,14)=2.07, p=0.17, ηp2 = 0.13), PRC-inhibited animals spent significantly longer in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair compared with trials completed without inhibition (laser off; p<0.001), and compared to GFP control animals (p<0.005) with laser on and off (laser × construct: F(1,14)=14.98, p=0.002, ηp2 = 0.52) (Figure 7d).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows significant effect of PRC inhibition on time in outcome-associated area.

claim: Laser treatment both decreased escape latency and increased cumulative duration in the outcome-associated area for ArchT animals compared with GFP in the shuttle box control cohort.
source: An analysis of the difference score of the two conflict test sessions (laser on–laser off) revealed that laser treatment both decreased escape latency (ArchT: 33.93±10.09, GFP: –1.02±10.14, t(14) = 6.91, p<0.001), and increased cumulative duration in the outcome-associated area (ArchT: 35.55±19.35, GFP: 3.21±13.58, t(14) = 6.91, p<0.001 t(14)=3.87, p=0.002) for ArchT animals compared with GFP.
evidence: Statistical comparisons of difference scores demonstrate specific effects in ArchT group.

claim: The findings from the shuttle box control cohort align with the data obtained from animals receiving continuous PRC inhibition throughout the shuttle box test, indicating that impairments in encoding or valence recall when faced with high motivational conflict are unlikely to contribute to the decreased avoidance behavior following PRC inhibition.
source: These findings align with the data obtained from animals receiving continuous PRC inhibition throughout the shuttle box test, indicating that impairments in encoding or valence recall when faced with high motivational conflict are unlikely to contribute to the decreased avoidance behavior following PRC inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary comparing results across experimental conditions.

claim: All rats acquired the cue-outcome associations successfully by test 2 in the Y-maze AA task, spending significantly more time in the appetitive arm and less time in the aversive arm compared with the neutral arm.
source: Analysis of time spent in a given arm after four (test 1) and eight (test 2) conditioning sessions, without laser treatment, revealed that all rats acquired the cue-outcome associations successfully by test 2 (valence: F(2,32)=146.02, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.9; valence × test: F(2,32)=24.26, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.6), regardless of construct (construct: F(1,16)=0.17, p=0.69, ηp2 = 0.01; test × construct: F(1,16) = 0.01, p=0.92, ηp2 = 0.001; valence × construct: F(2,32)=1.51, p=0.24, ηp2 = 0.09) by spending significantly more time in the appetitive arm (both tests p<0.001) and less time in the aversive arm (both p≤0.003) compared with the neutral arm (Figure 8b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition in Y-maze task.

claim: PRC inhibition did not significantly change the time spent in either arm during the Y-maze conflict test.
source: Rats then completed two AA conflict tests during which they could freely explore between a conflict arm containing a combination of appetitive and aversive cues, and a neutral arm containing the neutral cue. PRC inhibition did not significantly change the time spent in either arm (laser: F(1,16) = 4.06, p=0.060, ηp2 = 0.2; laser × construct: F(1,16)=1.06, p=0.32, ηp2 = 0.06) (Figure 8c)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect of PRC inhibition in Y-maze conflict test.

claim: Both ArchT and GFP animals spent a comparable duration of time in both the conflict and neutral arms in the Y-maze task.
source: and both ArchT and GFP animals spent a comparable duration of time in both the conflict and neutral arms (arm: F(1,16)=0.09, p=0.77, ηp2 = 0.005; construct: F(1,16)=0.31, p=0.58, ηp2 = 0.02; arm × construct: F(1,16)=2.47, p=0.14, ηp2 = 0.13).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no differences in arm preference.

claim: PRC inhibition did not significantly alter the number of entries made into or retreats from either the conflict or neutral arms in the Y-maze task.
source: Moreover, PRC inhibition did not significantly alter the number of entries made into or retreats from either the conflict or neutral arms (entries: laser: F(1,16)=0.001, p=0.98, ηp2 <0.001; construct: F(1,16)=3.36, p=0.09, ηp2 = 0.17; laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.07, p=0.8, ηp2 = 0.004; retreats: laser: F(1,16)=0.03, p=0.86, ηp2 = 0.002; construct: F(1,16)=0.5, p=0.49, ηp2 = 0.3; laser × construct: F(1,16)=0.2, p=0.66, ηp2 = 0.12) (Figure 8d–e).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on entries or retreats in Y-maze task.

claim: The number of entries and retreats did not differ between conflict and neutral arms for both ArchT and GFP animals in the Y-maze task.
source: The number of entries and retreats also did not differ between conflict and neutral arms (entries: arm: F(1,16)=0.001, p=0.98, ηp2 <0.001; retreats: arm: F(1,16)=1.19, p=0.29, ηp2 = 0.07) for both ArchT and GFP animals (entries: arm × construct F(1,16)=0.07, p=0.8, ηp2 = 0.004; retreats: arm × construct: F(1,16)=0.43, p=0.52, ηp2 = 0.03).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no differences in behavior between arms.

claim: While PRC is critical for AA conflict processing associated with discrete objects, it may play a minimal role in contextual AA conflict.
source: Thus, while PRC is critical for AA conflict processing associated with discrete objects, it may play a minimal role in contextual AA conflict.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the Y-maze results showing no effect of PRC inhibition.

claim: vCA3 rats demonstrated successful valence learning across the two acquisition tests in the object runway paradigm.
source: vCA3 rats demonstrated successful valence learning across the two acquisition tests (valence: F(2,26)=160.44, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.93; valence × test: F(2,26)=23.73, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.65) (Figure 9b)
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition in vCA3 rats.

claim: At test 2, vCA3 rats spent the most time in the goal box after appetitive object exposure and the least time after aversive object exposure in comparison to neutral trials.
source: and at test 2 spent the most time in the goal box after appetitive object exposure and the least time after aversive object exposure in comparison to neutral trials (both p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparisons demonstrate successful valence learning.

claim: Object valence acquisition was similar for ArchT and GFP animals in the vCA3 group, with the exception that ArchT rats spent less time in the goal box compared to GFP rats during acquisition test 1.
source: Object valence acquisition was similar for ArchT and GFP animals (construct: F(1,13)=3.85, p=0.07, ηp2 = 0.23; valence × construct: F(2,26)=0.20, p=0.82, ηp2 = 0.02) with the exception that ArchT rats spent less time in the goal box compared to GFP rats during acquisition test 1 (test × construct: F(1,13)=7.13, p=0.019, ηp2 = 0.35; test 1 construct: F(1,13)=10.94, p=0.006, ηp2 = 0.46).
evidence: Statistical results show generally similar acquisition with one exception at test 1.

claim: ArchT and GFP animals did not differ at the end of training (test 2) in the vCA3 group.
source: ArchT and GFP animals did not, however, differ at the end of training (test 2 construct: F(1,13)=2.21, p=0.16, ηp2 = 0.15).
evidence: Non-significant statistical result indicates no group difference at end of training.

claim: There was no effect of vCA3 inhibition on time spent in the goal box in the high conflict test session.
source: In contrast to PRC inhibition, there was no effect of vCA3 inhibition on time spent in the goal box in the high conflict test session (laser: F(1,13)=2.92, p=0.11, ηp2 = 0.18; construct: F(1,13)=0.001, p=0.99, ηp2 <0.001; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.93, p=0.60, ηp2 = 0.02) (Figure 9c).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect of vCA3 inhibition on high conflict behavior.

claim: An overall comparison across regions revealed that the impact of laser manipulation was significantly different between PRC and vCA3 animals in the runway high conflict test.
source: Indeed, an overall comparison across regions revealed that the impact of laser manipulation was significantly different between PRC and vCA3 animals (laser × region × construct: F(1,29)=22.83, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.44).
evidence: Statistical comparison demonstrates differential effects between brain regions.

claim: vCA3 inhibition did not impact the number of retreats, entries made into the goal box, or latency to enter in the high conflict test.
source: vCA3 inhibition also did not impact other behavioral measures (Figure 9d) including the number of retreats (laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.03, p=0.86, ηp2 = 0.003), entries made into the goal box (laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.58, p=0.46, ηp2 = 0.04), and LTE (laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.37, p=0.55, ηp2 = 0.03).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effects on multiple behavioral measures.

claim: vCA3 inhibition did not affect time spent in the goal box when rodents were presented with the neutral object pair.
source: vCA3 inhibition also did not affect time spent in the goal box when rodents were presented with the neutral object pair (laser: F(1,11)=0.03, p=0.90, ηp2 = 0.03; laser × construct: F(1,11)=2.36, p=0.15, ηp2 = 0.18) (Figure 9e).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect in neutral condition.

claim: vCA3 inhibition did not impact the time spent in the goal box during the low conflict test.
source: Similar to the high conflict test, vCA3 inhibition did not impact the time spent in the goal box during the low conflict test (laser: F(1,13)=0.11, p=0.75, ηp2 = 0.008; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.29, p=0.60, ηp2 = 0.02) (Figure 9f)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect in low conflict condition.

claim: There was a significant difference between vCA3 and PRC rats when compared directly in the low conflict test.
source: and crucially, there was a significant difference between vCA3 and PRC rats when compared directly (laser × area × construct: F(1,25)=5.13, p=0.032, ηp2 = 0.17).
evidence: Statistical comparison demonstrates differential effects between brain regions in low conflict.

claim: All vCA3 animals could readily discriminate between valences as reflected by time spent in the goal box and retreats in the low conflict test.
source: All vCA3 animals could readily discriminate between valences as reflected by time spent in the goal box (valence: F(1,13)=550.18, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.98; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.25, p=0.63, ηp2 = 0.02) and retreats (valence: F(1,13)=13.80, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.52).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in vCA3 rats.

claim: There was no effect of vCA3 inhibition on entries into and retreats from the goal box in the low conflict test.
source: There was, however, no effect of vCA3 inhibition on entries into and retreats from the goal box (both valence × construct: F(1,13)≤0.55, p≥0.47, ηp2≤ 0.09) (Figure 9g–h).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on entries or retreats.

claim: Following successful acquisition of a new set of appetitive and aversive object pairs, vCA3 inhibition did not impact time spent in the goal box in the within-valence no conflict recombination test.
source: Following successful acquisition of a new set of appetitive and aversive object pairs (valence: F(1,13)=361.37, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; pairing: F(1,13)=0.006, p=0.94, ηp2 <0.001; valence × pairing: F(1,13)=0.19, p=0.67, ηp2 = 0.02; pairing × construct: F(1, 13)=0.14, p=0.72, ηp2 = 0.01) (Figure 9i), vCA3 inhibition also did not impact time spent in the goal box in the within-valence no conflict recombination test (laser: F(1,13)=0.14, p=0.72, ηp2=0.01; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.040, p=0.85, ηp2 = 0.003) (Figure 9j)
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect in no conflict condition.

claim: Entries into and retreats from the goal box were unaffected by vCA3 inhibition in the no conflict test.
source: with entries into and retreats from the goal box also unaffected (both valence × construct: F(1,13)≤1.10, p≥0.31, ηp2≤ 0.2) (Figure 9k–l).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on entries or retreats.

claim: Both ArchT and GFP animals could discriminate between the two valences by spending more time in the goal box and retreating less for appetitive pairs compared to aversive pairs in the vCA3 no conflict test.
source: Both ArchT and GFP animals could discriminate between the two valences by spending more time in the goal box and retreating less for appetitive pairs compared to aversive pairs (valence: F(1,13)=481.57, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.03, p=0.88, ηp2 = 0.002).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination.

claim: vCA3 inhibition had no impact on any aspect of performance on the object AA runway task.
source: In sum, vCA3 inhibition had no impact on any aspect of performance on the object AA runway task.
evidence: This is a summary statement of all the vCA3 runway results.

claim: All vCA3 rats demonstrated successful establishment of an active avoidance response toward aversive, but not appetitive object pairings, across two acquisition tests in the shuttle box task.
source: vCA3 rats also completed the object-based shuttle box, and all rats demonstrated successful establishment of an active avoidance response toward aversive, but not appetitive object pairings, across two acquisition tests, exhibiting significantly shorter escape latencies after exposure to the aversive object pair compared with exposure to the appetitive object pair (valence: F(1,13)=119.71, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.90; valence × test: F(1,13)=92.12, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.88; construct: F(1,13)=1.43, p=0.25, ηp2 = 0.10; valence × construct: F(1,13)=1.18, p=0.30, ηp2 = 0.08; test × construct: F(1,13)=0.03, p=0.87, ηp2 = 0.002) (Figure 10a).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates successful acquisition in vCA3 shuttle box task.

claim: All vCA3 rats spent more in the outcome-associated area when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair in the shuttle box task.
source: All vCA3 rats also spent more in the outcome-associated area when exposed to the appetitive object pair compared with the aversive object pair (valence: F(1,13)=384.84, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.97; valence × test: F(1,13)=9.41, p=0.0090, ηp2 = 0.42; construct: F(1,13)=0.01, p=0.98, ηp2 < 0.001; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.68, p=0.42, ηp2 = 0.05; test × construct: F(1,13)=1.28, p=0.28, ηp2 = 0.09) (Figure 10b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates differential stay behavior based on valence.

claim: There was no effect of vCA3 inhibition on escape latency behavior when exposed to the high conflict object pairing in the shuttle box task.
source: In contrast to PRC rats, there was no effect of vCA3 inhibition on escape latency behavior when exposed to the high conflict object pairing (laser: F(1,13)=0.48, p=0.5, ηp2 = 0.04; construct: F(1,13)=0.03, p=0.87, ηp2 = 0.002; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.29, p=0.87, ηp2 = 0.02) (Figure 10c).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect of vCA3 inhibition on escape latency.

claim: An overall comparison across regions revealed that the impact of laser manipulation was significantly different between PRC and vCA3 animals in the shuttle box high conflict test.
source: An overall comparison across regions revealed that the impact of laser manipulation was significantly different between PRC and vCA3 animals (laser × region × construct: F(1,22)=13.78, p=0.0012, ηp2 = 0.39).
evidence: Statistical comparison demonstrates differential effects between brain regions in shuttle box.

claim: vCA3 inhibition had no effect on the time spent in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair in the shuttle box task.
source: vCA3 inhibition also had no effect on the time spent in the outcome-associated area containing the conflict object pair (laser: F(1,13)=0.26, p=0.62, ηp2 = 0.02; construct: F(1,13)=0.12, p=0.74, ηp2 = 0.009; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.020, p=0.89, ηp2 = 0.002) (Figure 10d).
evidence: Non-significant statistical results indicate no effect on time in outcome-associated area.

claim: There was a significant difference between vCA3 and PRC animals when compared directly in the shuttle box time spent in outcome-associated area measure.
source: Similarly, there was a significant difference between vCA3 and PRC animals when compared directly (laser × region × construct: F(1,22)=7.98, p=0.010, ηp2 = 0.27).
evidence: Statistical comparison demonstrates differential effects between brain regions.

claim: vCA3 inhibition had no effect on the duration of escape latencies for either appetitive or aversive valences during the control acquisition tests in the shuttle box task.
source: vCA3 inhibition also had no effect on the duration of escape latencies for either appetitive or aversive valences during the control acquisition tests (laser: F(1,13)=0.51, p=0.49, ηp2 = 0.04; laser × construct: F(1,13)=3.13, p=0.1, ηp2 = 0.19; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.25, p=0.63, ηp2 = 0.02), with all rats exhibiting significantly shorter escape latencies for aversive than appetitive trials (valence: F(1,13)=826.68, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.99; construct: F(1,13)=0.03, p=0.88, ηp2 = 0.002) (Figure 10e).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in shuttle box control test.

claim: vCA3 inhibition had no effect on the amount of time spent in the cued side of the apparatus during the shuttle box control test.
source: Similarly, vCA3 inhibition had no effect on the amount of time spent in the cued side of the apparatus (laser: F(1,13)=0.86, p=0.37, ηp2 = 0.06; laser × construct: F(1,13)=0.04, p=0.84, ηp2 = 0.003; valence × construct: F(1,13)=0.69, p=0.42, ηp2 = 0.05), with all rats spending significantly less time in the cued side during aversive than appetitive trials (valence: F(1,13)=565.77, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.98; construct: F(1,13)=0.30, p=0.59, ηp2 = 0.02) (Figure 10f).
evidence: Statistical results demonstrate intact valence discrimination in shuttle box control test.

claim: vCA3 inhibition had no impact on object-associated motivational behavior whether under AA conflict or the presence of appetitive or aversive cues alone.
source: In sum, these results indicate that vCA3 inhibition had no impact on object-associated motivational behavior whether under AA conflict or the presence of appetitive or aversive cues alone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of all the vCA3 shuttle box results.

claim: Laser-treated PRC ArchT animals exhibited a significant NOR impairment compared with laser-off ArchT and PRC-GFP control animals.
source: For the NOR task, an analysis of the discrimination ratio (difference between novel and familiar object exploration divided by total exploration) revealed that laser-treated PRC ArchT animals exhibited a significant NOR impairment (laser: F(1,34)=45.6, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.57, construct: F(1,34)=28.46, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.46; laser × construct: F(1,34)=39.63, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.54) (Figure 11a) compared with laser-off ArchT and PRC-GFP control animals (all p≤0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates impairment in novel object recognition with PRC inhibition.

claim: Laser-treated vCA3-ArchT animals spent a significantly increased proportion of time in the open arms of the EPM compared with laser-off ArchT and vCA3-GFP control animals.
source: In the EPM, laser-treated vCA3-ArchT animals spent a significantly increased proportion of time in the open arms (laser: F(1,11)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.42; construct: F(1,11)=14.42, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.57; laser × construct: F(1,11) = 7.1, p=0.022, ηp2 = 0.39) compared with laser-off Arch T and vCA3-GFP control animals (all p≤0.001) (Figure 11b).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates anxiolytic effect of vCA3 inhibition in EPM.

claim: ArchT animals that completed either the NOR or EPM tasks with the laser on prior to sacrifice demonstrated a significant reduction in cFos labeling in the PRC or vCA3, compared with ArchT animals that completed the tasks with laser off and GFP control animals.
source: ArchT animals that completed either the NOR (PRC) or EPM (vCA3) tasks with the laser on prior to sacrifice demonstrated a significant reduction in cFos labeling in the PRC (laser: F(1,34)=98.11, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.74; construct: F(1,34)=56.49, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.62; laser × construct: F(1,34)=64.82, p<0.0001, ηp2 = 0.66) or vCA3 (laser: F(1,11)=5.81, p=0.035, ηp2 = 0.35; construct: F(1,11)=3.77, p=0.07, ηp2 = 0.26; laser × construct: F(1,11)=12.78, p=0.004; ηp2 = 0.54), compared with ArchT animals that completed the tasks with laser off and GFP control animals (all p≤0.001) (Figure 11c–e).
evidence: Statistical analysis demonstrates reduced neural activation with optogenetic inhibition.

claim: Laser treatment in ArchT animals significantly reduced neural activation.
source: Thus, laser treatment in ArchT animals significantly reduced neural activation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the cFos results.

claim: Histological analysis confirmed robust bilateral expression of GFP/ArchT and optic fiber tip placement immediately dorsal to the viral injection site in all PRC animals.
source: Finally, histological analysis confirmed robust bilateral expression of GFP/ArchT and optic fiber tip placement immediately dorsal to the viral injection site in all PRC animals (Figure 11).
evidence: Histological verification confirms proper viral expression and fiber placement.

claim: No exclusions were made based on optic fiber placement/viral expression in the PRC group.
source: Thus, no exclusions were made based on optic fiber placement/viral expression.
